Name: filler_token_computation
Title: Do Reasoning Models Compute in Filler Tokens? Mechanistic Evidence for Hidden Computation
Short Hypothesis: A substantial fraction of tokens in long chain-of-thought traces are computationally inert 'filler': the residual stream at these positions carries little task-relevant information, and the model's forward pass could skip them without accuracy loss. We can mechanistically identify which tokens carry computation versus which are surface decoration, enabling principled trace compression.
Related Work: Pfau et al. (2024) show filler tokens ('...') can help on parallelizable tasks; Lanham et al. (2023) study CoT faithfulness; Wang et al. (2024) show CoT compression via prompting. Prior work is behavioral. We differ by giving a mechanistic, per-token diagnostic (attribution + causal ablation) that predicts which tokens are computationally load-bearing, rather than measuring aggregate accuracy after perturbation.
Abstract: Reasoning-tuned language models emit long chain-of-thought (CoT) traces, but it is unclear whether every token performs computation or many are surface filler. We propose a mechanistic per-token diagnostic combining (i) attention attribution from the final answer back to each CoT token, (ii) residual-stream information probes measuring task-relevant content at each position, and (iii) causal token dropout that replaces a token's key/value with a neutral placeholder and measures answer change. We hypothesize a heavy-tailed distribution: a small set of 'load-bearing' tokens (numeric results, decisions, constraints) carries most computation, while connective and hedging tokens are near-inert. Across math and logic benchmarks we correlate the three signals and show they jointly predict which tokens can be pruned with negligible accuracy loss. We further test whether load-bearing status is predictable online from local activations, enabling a streaming compressor that halts or skips inert spans. Results would establish that CoT length is partly decorative and that mechanistic signals expose the true computational skeleton of reasoning, offering an interpretability-grounded route to efficient inference. Negative results (uniform computation across tokens) would themselves refine faithfulness debates.
Experiments: 1. Run DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B and Qwen3-8B on GSM8K, MATH, and a logic-grid set; save traces and per-layer activations. 2. Compute answer->token attention attribution (integrated gradients over attention) for each CoT token. 3. Train linear probes on residual stream to decode the final answer at each position; measure per-token task information. 4. Causal dropout: replace each token's KV with mean/pad KV, measure exact-match answer change. 5. Correlate the three signals (Spearman) and cluster tokens into load-bearing vs inert. 6. Prune high-inert tokens up to X% and re-run; plot accuracy vs compression. 7. Train a lightweight online classifier (logistic on layer-mid activations) to predict inert tokens without lookahead; evaluate streaming compression accuracy/latency.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Attribution methods are noisy and may disagree; causal dropout perturbs the KV distribution off-manifold. Inertness may be context-dependent so pruning could interact with later tokens. Findings may not transfer across model families or RL vs distillation training. Streaming prediction may be too weak to be practical.
